sources.title: University of Bath study warns AI could erode human capital, thinking and expertise in the workplace
sources.text:
AI may prove a double-edged sword in HR and people management





HR and people managers should proceed with caution if they want to use AI to improve efficiency and human capital in the workplace, and should take steps to ensure creativity and critical thinking are preserved, new research from the University of Bath School of Management shows.

“AI is widely promoted as a tool that can support employees by improving efficiency, speeding up problem solving and delivering personalised answers but this should not be taken at face value,” said Professor Dirk Lindebaum, author of the study 'On the Dangers of Large-Language Model Mediated Learning for Human Capital’.

“AI has a part to play in building human capital but it is vital to understand that human knowledge is not uniform. It comes in different kinds, some of which may be more compatible with AI than others,” Professor Lindebaum said.

The research team identified two types of knowledge which appeared partially compatible with AI - encoded knowledge, which encompasses rules, procedures, policies, and datasets; and embedded knowledge - essentially digitalised processes and routines.

“AI may support tasks in these areas by updating documents, policies and workflows, or assisting with compliance and this seems an obvious and easy win for a manager. However, it is not without risk - if employees, for example, no longer engage directly with important processes, familiarity and expertise will fade,” Professor Lindebaum said.

The team identified three forms of knowledge incompatible with AI: embodied knowledge - developed through practical, hands-on experience; encultured knowledge - understanding developed through organisational culture; and embrained knowledge - analytical judgment and problem-solving.

“These three forms of knowledge rely on real-world experience, sensory engagement, socialisation and repeated practice. They cannot be learned through exposure to AI-generated text or synthetic training environments,” Professor Lindebaum said.

“If people begin outsourcing thinking, decision-making or interpretation to AI systems, these critical forms of knowledge wither over time and create a dangerous dependency that could possibly compromise an organisation or a company’s profitability,” he added.

The researchers said HR and people managers need to safeguard against those risks by designing work that ensures continued access to first-hand learning and human interaction, such as shadowing or mentoring at work.

Additionally, they said cultural understanding should be underpinned by onboarding, team-based learning, cross-cultural exchanges and leadership modelling. And HR teams should encourage critical thinking and reflective practices as key skills in their employees to drive human-led decision making.

The research team suggested that critical thinking and creative skills could be safeguarded by created protected spaces within workplaces and educational settings - ‘learning vaults’.

Akin to the Svalbard Seed Vault which safeguards biodiversity, ‘learning vaults’ would be safeguarded from the influence of overly automated learning systems to help ensure employees develop adaptive, experience-based knowledge and maintain the reflexive capacities essential for forming human capital.

“In practise, that would mean a social environment in which employees and students learn how to think for themselves together in terms of know-why (e.g., why did the strategic plan fail?), know-how (e.g., how did a lack of local knowledge contribute to the failure?), and know-what (e.g., what are the consequences of said failure?),” Professor Lindebaum said.

“It would mean ‘learning the basics’ about tasks, processes and routines before cognitive offloading from the beginning undermines the ability of employees and students to provide informed answers about these questions. We think that employers and business schools should explore how such vaults can be integrated into roles and learning environments to protect diverse forms of knowledge that might otherwise be eroded by uncritical AI use,” Professor Lindebaum said.

sources.title: Case Studies: How is Generative AI being used at Bath?
sources.text:
Published on: 24/08/2023 · Last updated on: 02/09/2024
CLT EduTalk

Our CLT EduTalk in March 2023 focused on the current ‘hot topic’ in education – ChatGPT and the impact of generative artificial intelligence (AI). The CLT was pleased to welcome over 85 staff and students from across campus to the online event on 7 March, where colleagues from the Department for Health, the Department of Computer Science and the School of Management gave some excellent insights into the ways in which they have been working with generative AI in their teaching and scholarship. The talks below refer to ChatGPT-3.5.

Case Study 1: Evaluation of ChatGPT Capabilities

Joshua Evans, Department of Computer Science

Joshua gave an brief introduction to ChatGPT and outlined its’ capabilities. He has been looking at generative AI tools and considering them from the angle of academic integrity. Most recently, his focus has been to specifically evaluate ChatGPT’s performance at generating assessment responses.

Introduction to ChatGPT and its Capabilities

Case Study 2:Assignment audit using ChatGPT

James Fern, Department for Health

James has been carrying out an initial audit of a selection of current UG assignment questions/briefs. In his audit, he has been looking across the course years to identify how well ChatGPT answers the assessment questions posed at different levels.

ChatGPT Assessment Audit

Case Study 3:Harnessing ChatGPT as a tool to aid critical thinking

Kim Watts & Dr Carl-Philip Ahlbom, School of Management

Carl-Philip and Kim have been piloting use of ChatGPT as a tool to support the development of students’ higher order thinking skills (their ability to analyse, evaluate and synthesise) as part of their assessment. They have been engaging students in considering the limitations of the tool and the importance of promoting and harnessing human critical thinking.

Chat GPT Workshop

Case Study 4:ChatGPT – Reliance on Linguistic Form

Dr Harish Madabushi, Department of Computer Science

An extract from the work being carried out by Harish Madabushi in Computer Science, looking more closely at how ChatGPT functions.

ChatGPTs Reliance on Linguistic Form in Inferential Reasoning

sources.title: When Not to Use AI | Benjamin Laker
sources.text:
Topics




Column

Our expert columnists offer opinion and analysis on important issues facing modern businesses and managers.




More in this series














Carolyn Geason-Beissel/MIT SMR | Getty Images

Summary: AI may accelerate work, but it can’t lead people. MIT SMR columnist Benjamin Laker suggests leaving the mechanical tasks to artificial intelligence so that you can focus on the meaningful work — the work that requires the management skills at which humans excel. Rely on your own judgment to deliver messages and make decisions involving values, relationships, or trust, he advises. That’s your job as a manager, and a responsibility that should not be outsourced to AI.
AI promises to make managers more productive and give them access to more information more quickly. It can draft plans, summarize reports, and even coach you on how to deliver feedback. Yet the same technology that accelerates decision-making can also erode your judgment, if you let it. Rely on artificial intelligence too little, and you miss its advantages. Rely on it too much, and you risk delegating your thinking instead of sharpening it.
Leading well in the age of AI is about balance. You need to know when to let algorithms lighten the load — and when to carry the weight on your own shoulders so your judgment stays strong.
Where AI Helps You Think Faster
AI excels at compressing time. It can scan vast quantities of information, synthesize key points, and produce first drafts of documents or presentations in seconds. Used wisely, AI accelerates the slowest parts of managerial work: gathering data, preparing materials, and finding patterns.
When time is tight, use AI to handle the groundwork so that you can focus on sensemaking. Let it outline a report so that you can spend your energy on the real managerial work: deciding what findings matter, what signals to prioritize, and what the implications are for strategy or next steps. Have it summarize team feedback so that you can concentrate on what action to take. Use it to prepare talking points for a performance review, and then spend your time planning your tone and delivery. This keeps you in the driver’s seat of decisions rather than buried in prep work.



The key is to treat AI’s output as raw material, not finished work. Skim it, shape it, and then make it yours. If you publish or present it exactly as generated, you are not accelerating your thinking — you are bypassing it. The goal is speed with discernment, not speed alone.
Where AI Can Quiet Your Judgment
The danger comes when speed begins to replace scrutiny. AI makes suggestions confidently, even when they are shallow or wrong. It can lull you into skipping the second look you would normally take, which will dull your judgment over time.
This risk of using AI is highest when you are making decisions that depend on values, nuance, or relationships — precisely the work that defines good management. AI cannot sense the emotional weight of a change announcement, the politics around a promotion, or the fragility of a struggling employee’s confidence. It will give you an answer with no sense of the human context.
In hiring, for example, AI can short-list resumes in seconds, but it cannot gauge a candidate’s resilience based on how they talk about a setback during an interview. When it comes to strategy development, AI can surface competitive trends, but it cannot sense how your team will emotionally react to a bold new direction. In these moments, your presence matters more than your productivity.
If you notice yourself accepting AI’s outputs without editing them, slow down. Ask yourself: Would I stand by this recommendation if my name were on it alone? Would I say it out loud to someone I respect? Those questions reinsert accountability — and accountability sharpens judgment.

Putting AI in Its Place
You have the opportunity to make deliberate choices about how and when artificial intelligence can best serve you and your team. Here are three ways to make the most of AI — and your own skills.
Automate Tasks, Not Trust
A practical way to stay balanced is to divide your work into tasks and trust. Tasks are the repeatable processes that benefit from speed. Trust is the human currency of management — the beliefs, emotions, and loyalties that bind a team together.
Use AI on tasks. Let it draft timelines, crunch numbers, or generate slides. Do not use it where trust is paramount. Deliver feedback yourself. Write the opening paragraph of a promotion announcement in your own voice. Decide when to change a goal or approve a hire with your own mind engaged, not on autopilot.
This distinction keeps AI working as your tool, not your proxy. It does the mechanical work while you do the meaningful work.
Consider your weekly team meeting. AI can help you build the agenda, surface metrics, and compile questions from your team’s project boards. But the tone of that meeting — whether people feel heard, valued, and motivated — is yours alone to create. No algorithm can do that for you. When trust is at stake, resist the urge to outsource.
Use AI to Widen Perspective, Not Narrow It
Another trap is using AI only to confirm what you already believe. Because these tools are designed to be agreeable, they will happily produce arguments that support your instincts. This can make you feel more decisive while actually limiting the options you consider.

When trust is at stake, resist the urge to outsource.

To avoid getting stuck in your own ideas, occasionally instruct AI to make a counterargument to your preferred option. If you are leaning toward reorganizing a team, ask for reasons not to. If you are ready to approve a budget, ask for the strongest case to reject it. This will force you to confront counterarguments before you commit — and it protects you from becoming overly certain about a decision simply because a machine echoed your view.
The best managers use AI to challenge their thinking, not to cushion it. They treat it as a sparring partner, not a cheerleader.
Build a Personal Guardrail

Even experienced managers can slip from using AI wisely to leaning on it too heavily. The shift is subtle — and it often feels like efficiency. To prevent that, build a simple guardrail: Track how much of your day involves thinking that you could not delegate. Ask yourself: Did I use AI to enhance my thinking or replace it? Did I exercise my judgment critically, or did I accept recommendations more automatically? These questions force you to notice the slope before you slide.
Some leaders set time blocks for “AI-free thinking” each week — no prompts, no tools, just unstructured reflection. Others limit AI use to specific tasks and keep a manual list of decisions where they want to feel the full weight of responsibility. Whatever the method you choose, the point is to keep drawing on your own judgment and critical thinking.

Thriving in the AI era does not mean adopting it fastest but remaining unmistakably human while using it. AI can accelerate your work, but it cannot care. It can generate options, but it cannot hold responsibility. That is your job — and the more AI can do for you, the more deliberate you must be about what you still do yourself. Let the machine do the lifting, not the leading.

sources.title: The Complementarity Paradox: Human-AI Collaboration, Overreliance, and Skill Decline in Entrepreneurial Contexts
sources.text:
1 IntroductionGenAI, a class of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models capable of generating meaningful content such as text, images, and audio (Banh & Strobel, 2023; Susarla et al., 2023), has shifted from a computer science milestone to a staple of everyday knowledge work. Professionals now routinely work alongside GenAI tools in arrangements increasingly described as human-AI collaboration (Seeber et al., 2020; Vössing et al., 2022).Early evidence shows that GenAI tools can meaningfully augment individual task performance (Dell’Acqua et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2023), fuelling rapid organizational uptake. Firms are increasingly integrating GenAI into customer operations, marketing and sales, software engineering, and product-development workflows, reflecting a broader shift from experimental use toward enterprise-scale deployment and strategic investment (Capgemini & Microsoft, 2024; Chui et al., 2023; Research and Markets, 2025). Entrepreneurs, for their part, use the same tools to level the playing field against larger incumbents (Calvino et al., 2025), configuring human-AI collaboration arrangements that reshape task boundaries.Whether GenAI ultimately strengthens or erodes professional capability remains an open question, and the evidence so far points in both directions. A substantial body of work documents augmentation effects. GenAI tools have been shown to improve task performance, raise output quality, and disproportionately benefit lower-skilled workers, thereby democratizing access to expertise (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025; Dell’Acqua et al., 2023; Noy & Zhang, 2023). GenAI functions as a scaffold that lifts capability floors and may even accelerate skill acquisition for those still developing their competence.A counter-account, grounded in cognitive offloading theory (Risko & Gilbert, 2016) and the automation-induced deskilling literature (Bainbridge, 1983; Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010), emphasizes that the same delegation mechanisms associated with short-run productivity gains may also reduce opportunities for effortful retrieval and rehearsal over time. Both accounts can be true for different users, tasks, and time horizons. However, we lack understanding of how individual-level factors shape the conditions under which GenAI use enhances versus undermines skill development. Entrepreneurial cognition, encompassing the cognition structures, heuristics, and mental models entrepreneurs use to recognize, evaluate, and exploit opportunities (Baron, 2004; Mitchell et al., 2002), provides a theoretically consequential setting in which to examine how sustained GenAI use may affect professional capability.In this context, Individual Entrepreneurial Orientation (IEO), a dispositional trait reflecting innovativeness, proactiveness, and calculated risk-taking (Bolton & Lane, 2012; Lumpkin & Dess, 1996), may influence the extent to which individuals embed GenAI in their professional work. An entrepreneurial appetite for experimentation accelerates adoption, but it can also set in motion a less desirable dynamic in which intensive GenAI use fosters GenAI dependence, which in turn is associated with a perceived erosion of underlying skills.This dynamic is particularly pronounced as collaboration deepens, and especially so among individuals with a strong long-term orientation (LTO), who tend to view GenAI as a durable strategic resource and govern their engagement with it on a longer time horizon (Bearden et al., 2006; Hofstede, 2001). Although prior work links IEO to technology adoption and firm performance, it has not examined how IEO-driven GenAI usage can paradoxically undermine the very skills entrepreneurs rely on through specific human-AI collaboration configurations (Vössing et al., 2022). Our study investigates one specific slice of this broader question through the following research question (RQ):

RQ: How do individual entrepreneurial orientation and long-term orientation shape the extent to which GenAI use translates into GenAI Dependence and perceived skill atrophy?

We do not argue that GenAI use inevitably produces dependence or skill decline; rather, we examine the individual-level conditions under which a beneficial collaboration arrangement may drift toward dependence and perceived skill atrophy. To address our RQ, we draw on data from a two-wave survey of 143 knowledge workers in five countries and anchor our arguments in two complementary theoretical foundations. Cognitive offloading theory (Risko & Gilbert, 2016) explains why individuals externalize memory and cognitive steps to reliable tools, and predicts that such delegation, although efficient in the short run, routinizes reliance and gradually fosters GenAI dependence. Skill decay theory (Arthur Jr et al., 1998), reinforced by the automation-induced deskilling tradition (Bainbridge, 1983; Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010), explains why sustained non-use of a capability leads to its deterioration: when effortful retrieval is consistently bypassed, the memory representations and procedural schemas that sustain expertise are progressively weakened. Together, these two pillars suggest that the short-term efficiency gains associated with GenAI use may translate, through dependence, into a longer-term erosion of the rehearsal cycles on which professional skill depends.By integrating cognitive offloading theory and skill decay theory into the study of human-AI collaboration, we illuminate the mechanism by which voluntary offloading may become obligatory dependence and become associated with perceived erosion of professional skills, and we surface the conditions under which complementarity may shade into perceived substitution. By uncovering how individual entrepreneurial and temporal mind-sets can convert GenAI’s short-run efficiency into perceived long-run capability vulnerability, the study advances theory on human-AI collaboration and entrepreneurial cognition, and contributes to scholarship on digital work configurations.This study advances Information Systems (IS) scholarship by demonstrating that the consequences of GenAI adoption are not reducible to mere system utilization. Rather, outcomes are shaped by the degree to which human-AI collaboration arrangements become behaviourally routinized and psychologically internalized within professional work contexts.The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 situates the study within the existing literature and develops its theoretical foundations in human-AI collaboration and digital work configurations. Section 3 articulates the hypotheses and presents the research model. Section 4 describes the measurement design and data-collection procedures. Section 5 sets out the analytical strategy and reports the tests of the hypothesized relationships. Section 6 interprets the empirical findings, and Section 7 draws out their theoretical and managerial implications. Section 8 acknowledges the study’s limitations, Section 9 outlines directions for future research, and the final section offers concluding observations.2 Background Literature and Theoretical Underpinnings2.1 Generative AI and its Impact on Individual Skill TrajectoriesThe emergence of GenAI represents a paradigm shift in knowledge work and in human-AI collaboration, revolutionizing how professionals identify opportunities, execute tasks, and accelerate their productivity (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025; Dell’Acqua et al., 2023; Noy & Zhang, 2023). Unlike earlier forms of automation that primarily targeted routine tasks, GenAI systems such as ChatGPT, DALL-E, and Claude can augment, and in some task contexts partially substitute for, human intellectual capabilities (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025; Eloundou et al., 2023). We argue that this fundamental shift carries significant implications for how professional skills are developed, applied, and retained over time. As organizations increasingly integrate GenAI into everyday workflows, it becomes critical to examine its effects not only on immediate task performance but also on the development and retention of professional skills, the evolution of expertise, and longer-term trajectories of individual capability (Lebovitz et al., 2021; Raisch & Krakowski, 2021). We conceptualize GenAI usage as the depth of human-AI collaboration: the extent to which AI participation is embedded in task cycles within digital work configurations. Parallel work on digital productivity assistants shows how such tools can reshape work patterns, redistribute responsibility for productivity, and introduce new questions of workload negotiation and organizational control in knowledge work, underscoring that collaboration depth is partly a governance decision rather than a purely technical one (Nyman et al., 2024). To ground this framing, we build on two streams. First, IS scholarship, with related insights from human-computer interaction, conceptualizes human-AI work arrangements as varying in the degree of AI involvement, from occasional assistance to deeper forms of co-production, with implications for how tasks and decision-making responsibilities are allocated between humans and AI (Dellermann et al., 2019; Seeber et al., 2020).Second, technology engagement research has long held that use is multidimensional and not captured by frequency alone, but also by the extent to which a technology becomes embedded in users’ routines and experiences (Ellison et al., 2007). Drawing on both streams, we operationalize collaboration depth through two facets: behavioral engagement (time spent working with GenAI on professional tasks) and psychological embedding (the extent to which GenAI use is integrated into daily routines and work-related identity). We use the term depth rather than intensity to signal that what matters for downstream dependence and skill outcomes is not only how much GenAI is used but also how centrally it features in the user’s work. Accordingly, collaboration depth in the present study refers to the behavioral and psychological embeddedness of GenAI use rather than to the detailed allocation of tasks or contributions between the human and the system.Recent empirical studies have documented the rapid diffusion of GenAI across a range of professional domains, including software development (Peng et al., 2023), management consulting (Dell’Acqua et al., 2023), creative writing (Doshi & Hauser, 2024), customer service (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025), and academic research (Korinek, 2023). This growing body of evidence underscores GenAI’s transformative potential in enhancing productivity and efficiency in cognitively demanding tasks.Empirical evidence already points to substantial productivity gains at the task level. In controlled field experiments, Noy and Zhang (2023) showed that a conversational Large Language Model (LLM) improved mid-level professional writing performance, with productivity gains and quality improvements especially pronounced among lower-ability participants. Likewise, Peng et al. (2023) demonstrated that GitHub Copilot consistently accelerated software-development tasks, underscoring GenAI’s capacity to augment individual output across domains. Framed as human-AI collaboration, these results suggest that the use of GenAI can involve deeper forms of task engagement rather than mere tool use.However, these observed productivity gains may obscure potential long-term implications for skill development, including the risk of gradual skill atrophy (SA) among users. For example, Dell’Acqua et al. (2023) found that consultants relying on AI performed significantly worse on tasks beyond AI’s capabilities, often due to uncritical adoption of AI outputs. These findings raise concerns that uncritical reliance on AI may create training deficits over time. We therefore position short-run productivity gains as a property of collaboration depth, with potential long-run costs when human-AI collaboration drifts toward asymmetric dependence.In this study, we treat collaboration depth as the perceived and behaviourally reported depth of GenAI engagement, while recognizing that future work could capture more task-structural indicators such as prompt-iteration patterns, task variety, workflow interdependence, and token-level trace data.2.2 Entrepreneurial Orientation and Technology EngagementThe entrepreneurial orientation characterized by innovativeness, proactiveness, and risk-taking propensity (Covin & Wales, 2012) fundamentally shapes how individuals engage with emerging technologies. McGrath and MacMillan (2000) further frame the entrepreneurial mindset as a cognitive lens through which individuals rapidly sense, act, and mobilize under uncertainty. At the individual level, this orientation is typically operationalized as IEO, a dispositional trait that captures these same three dimensions as stable habits of thought and action in decision-making (Bolton & Lane, 2012).Individuals high in IEO tend to experiment with and adopt novel tools, particularly under conditions of uncertainty or dynamism (Bolton & Lane, 2012). Prior research on entrepreneurial cognition has shown how prior knowledge, cognitive frameworks, and learning processes shape the way individuals identify and act on technology-related opportunities (Corbett, 2005; Shane, 2000). In the digital context, this disposition manifests as technology opportunism, the ability to sense and respond to emerging technological possibilities (Srinivasan et al., 2002). Building on this work, we argue that IEO functions as a configuration logic for human-AI collaboration, shaping what tasks are delegated to GenAI, when outputs are verified, and how handoffs between human and model are organized. This configuration logic tends to deepen collaboration rather than keep it episodic.Evidence shows that GenAI can reduce the time and effort required for creative and analytical tasks, professional writing, and software development (Dell’Acqua et al., 2023; Noy & Zhang, 2023; Peng et al., 2023). These efficiency gains may make GenAI a relatively low-friction tool for entrepreneurial experimentation. Research on entrepreneurial action adds a further element, suggesting that entrepreneurs often manage uncertainty by limiting their commitments to resources they can afford to lose (Sarasvathy, 2001, 2008). Together, these observations position GenAI as a low-friction, potentially high-upside tool that entrepreneurially oriented individuals may be willing to experiment with intensively. While this experimentation-oriented stance may accelerate GenAI integration, it may also heighten vulnerability to dependence, since short-term productivity gains can obscure longer-term implications for skill.Having argued that entrepreneurial orientation shapes GenAI engagement, we pause to acknowledge the directionality of this claim. The IEO-to-GenAI relationship we test here is one of two plausible directions. Recent work has documented a reverse channel, in which exposure to GenAI itself cultivates entrepreneurial dispositions and intentions (Duong, 2024; Duong & Nguyen, 2024). We focus on the forward channel, in which entrepreneurial disposition shapes GenAI engagement and its downstream capability consequences, because this is the channel most directly relevant to the paradox we set out to examine: why already-entrepreneurial users may experience erosion in the very capabilities that entrepreneurial dispositions are thought to cultivate. Disentangling the two channels empirically would require longitudinal or experimental designs. 2.3 Cognitive Offloading Theory and Skill RetentionCognitive offloading theory posits that humans will outsource memory storage, retrieval, and even higher-order reasoning to any external artefact that delivers the same outcome with less mental effort (Risko & Gilbert, 2016). Classic examples include grocery lists and smartphone reminders; GenAI is a far more powerful successor because it not only stores but also generates solutions. The immediate rewards of faster drafting, coding, or analysis, therefore, encourage users to delegate an ever-larger share of cognition to the model. While such delegation boosts short-run productivity, it simultaneously suppresses the rehearsal cycles and desirable difficulties that consolidate durable expertise (Bjork & Bjork, 2011). Over time, knowledge workers may experience an erosion of both declarative and procedural knowledge, a possibility that early neurophysiological evidence has begun to flag (Kosmyna et al., 2025). Evidence from generative settings has begun to accumulate. Lee et al. (2025) report that confidence in GenAI is associated with less enacted critical thinking, whereas task-specific self-confidence is associated with more, and that GenAI shifts critical thinking toward verification, response integration, and task stewardship rather than eliminating it. This pattern is consistent with our contention that capability consequences depend on the disposition and governance the user brings to the collaboration rather than on GenAI use as such. The evidence remains self-reported, however, and does not directly establish the downstream capability consequence.Within our focal context, cognitive offloading operates as the starting point of a three-step cascade. First, professionals high in IEO may engage with GenAI more intensively, using it for ideation, drafting, coding, and information gathering, thereby normalizing sustained tool use. Second, repeated delegation of memory search and reasoning tasks routinizes the offloading, so that what begins as convenient assistance can gradually harden into felt necessity, a state we refer to as GenAI dependence. Third, as reliance deepens, the space for rehearsal and deliberate practice narrows, and entrepreneurially oriented professionals may become vulnerable to perceived erosion of the professional skills they previously exercised independently, a pattern we describe as perceived SA. Conceptually, this describes a pathway from collaboration depth through collaboration asymmetry to perceived skill erosion, and specifies how usage intensity may, over time, translate into less visible perceptions of competence loss.2.4 Positioning GenAI Dependence within the Broader Technology-Dependence LiteratureConcerns about technology-induced dependence are neither new nor unique to GenAI. Each major wave of computing has raised similar questions about whether the technology in question would augment human capability or undermine it. Early work on industrial automation documented the paradox that replacing routine cognitive work with automated systems tended to erode the very skills operators needed in order to intervene when the automation failed (Bainbridge, 1983). The rise of internet search produced evidence of transactive memory offloading, with users showing poorer recall for information they believed would remain externally accessible, a pattern popularised as the Google effect (Sparrow et al., 2011). Carr (2008, 2014) generalized this argument across digital technologies, suggesting that sustained use of external cognitive aids reconfigures the human side of human-machine cognition. Smartphones have since been shown to fragment attention and to reduce working memory capacity, even when the device is not in active use (Ward et al., 2017). In each case, the dependence concern has turned out to be real but graduated, and the empirical record across technologies is mixed rather than uniformly negative.Two observations follow. First, dependence on cognitive aids is a structural feature of tool-mediated work rather than an incidental flaw of any particular technology. Cognitive offloading theory (Risko & Gilbert, 2016) formalizes this point. Whenever a reliable external artifact delivers the same cognitive output with less effort, users tend to offload. Second, and importantly for the present study, whether this offloading produces lasting capability loss depends both on what is being offloaded and on whether the user retains the effortful retrieval cycles that consolidate expertise (Bjork & Bjork, 2011). Calculators offloaded arithmetic without, on the whole, producing a durable numeracy decline in skilled users. Evidence from GPS use suggests that habitual reliance can affect spatial cognition in some contexts (Dahmani & Bohbot, 2020), illustrating that the consequences of cognitive aids may vary across functions and settings. The same tool can therefore be benign for one cognitive function and consequential for another.Against this backdrop, GenAI is theoretically distinctive on three grounds. Its cognitive reach, first, is broader than that of earlier technologies. Prior tools substituted for specific cognitive functions such as retrieval, arithmetic, wayfinding, or storage, whereas GenAI substitutes simultaneously for drafting, analysis, ideation, synthesis, and reasoning. The offloading is cross-cutting rather than domain-specific. Second, GenAI is generative rather than transactive. Earlier technologies externalized retrieval or computation and left interpretation to the user, while GenAI offloads the interpretation itself, including the synthesis steps through which professional expertise is typically consolidated. Third, the reasoning behind GenAI outputs remains opaque even when those outputs are plausible on their face, which raises the cost of verification and weakens the corrective feedback loops that might otherwise prevent usage from hardening into dependence. These features do not make GenAI categorically different from prior technologies. They do, however, locate it at a particularly consequential point on the offloading spectrum, where the cognitive work that sustains entrepreneurial expertise is most directly at stake. Our study builds on the broader technology-dependence tradition and extends it to a setting in which the distinctiveness of the technology plausibly amplifies the dependence dynamic it has long been shown to produce.2.5 Skill Decay and the Cost of DisuseCognitive offloading theory explains why individuals delegate mental effort to reliable external systems, but it says relatively little about why such delegation, sustained over time, should erode the underlying capabilities of the delegator. To anchor the downstream link in our model, we therefore draw on the skill decay and retention literature, together with the related work on automation-induced deskilling.Skill decay refers to the loss of trained knowledge and skills following a period of non-use or insufficient practice (Arthur Jr et al., 1998). In their meta-analytic review, Arthur and colleagues report substantial skill loss with non-use, with the magnitude of decay growing markedly as the non-practice interval lengthens, and identify task characteristics, particularly cognitive complexity, as a key moderator. Subsequent work in this tradition has identified the absence of rehearsal opportunities as a further predictor (e.g., Wang et al., 2013).The underlying mechanism is straightforward: professional skills, whether declarative or procedural, depend on retrieval and practice to remain consolidated, and when retrieval is consistently bypassed by an external agent, the memory representations and procedural schemas that sustain expertise are progressively weakened (Bjork & Bjork, 2011). This is more than ordinary forgetting; it reflects a gradual erosion of the cognitive structures on which skilled performance depends.The automation-induced deskilling literature extends this logic to technology-mediated work. In her well-known essay on the ironies of automation, Bainbridge (1983) observed that when operators delegate routine cognitive work to automated systems, they simultaneously forfeit the practice opportunities they need in order to intervene effectively when the automation fails or reaches its limits. A substantial body of subsequent research has documented this pattern across aviation, process control, and clinical decision-making, where reliance on automation has been shown to degrade both routine skill and the situational awareness that depends on active engagement with the task (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010; Parasuraman & Riley, 1997). GenAI appears to extend this logic to cognitive work. Once generative models absorb tasks such as drafting, analysis, and reasoning, the conditions that skill decay theory identifies as conducive to capability loss, namely sustained non-use and the absence of rehearsal, are at least partially reproduced in professional settings.The IS literature has observed a similar pattern in contexts involving cognitive, rather than physical, automation. Based on a sociotechnical case study of an accounting firm, Rinta-Kahila et al. (2023) explain skill erosion as arising from the interaction among automation reliance, complacency, and mindful conduct. As reliance on automation increases, complacency can develop at both the individual and organizational levels, gradually reducing workers’ attentiveness to their activities, efforts to maintain competence, and scrutiny of automated outputs. Their analysis is particularly relevant to our argument for two reasons. First, it identifies reliance, rather than the sheer frequency or intensity of technology use, as the more immediate source of skill erosion. Second, it suggests that this erosion may remain unnoticed by both employees and managers, which aligns with our conceptualization of dependence as a latent psychological state and skill atrophy as an outcome that may initially be recognized through users’ own perceptions.Cognitive offloading theory and skill decay theory thus serve as the two theoretical pillars of our model. The former explains the upstream mechanism through which intensive GenAI use translates into GenAI dependence; the latter explains the downstream mechanism through which sustained dependence is associated with perceived SA. This two-pillar architecture also helps to clarify why the short-run productivity gains attributable to GenAI may coexist with longer-run capability costs: the same delegation that reduces cognitive effort today removes the practice cycles on which tomorrow’s expertise depends.2.6 GenAI Dependence: Psychological and Behavioral PerspectivesWe define GenAI dependence as a felt psychological compulsion to engage with GenAI tools when completing professional tasks, even when those tasks could be completed without such assistance. This construct draws on two established traditions in the IS and human-computer interaction literatures: research on technology habit and compulsive use (Limayem et al., 2007; Turel & Serenko, 2012), and work on the cognitive and behavioral consequences of over-reliance on automated systems (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010; Parasuraman & Riley, 1997). A parallel literature is now developing dependence measures for AI systems rather than adapting instruments designed for earlier technologies. Li et al. (2025) draw on human-computer trust and addiction theory to validate an eighteen-item large language model (LLM) dependence scale, distinguishing functional from existential dependence. Goh et al. (2025), working within Goodman’s behavioral dependency framework, validated a Generative AI Dependency Scale across six studies and 1,333 participants, reporting a stable three-factor structure of cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences, and withdrawal. Our measure predates these instruments and follows the broader behavioral-dependence tradition. The adapted items capture affective discomfort when GenAI is unavailable, concern expressed by others, difficulty reducing use, concealment, and reliance on GenAI for tasks that could otherwise be completed independently. These concerns overlap with aspects of dependence subsequently identified by Goh et al. (2025), although we do not claim dimensional or item-level equivalence.In the GenAI context, dependence is likely to show up when users find it difficult to perform tasks they previously completed without AI assistance, experience reduced confidence in their own judgment, and default to AI-mediated solutions even for tasks within their established expertise. In human-AI collaboration terms, this reflects what we describe as collaboration asymmetry, a state in which the user experiences GenAI as increasingly indispensable to task completion and becomes less able or willing to complete work independently.The IS literature on habitual technology use offers a useful mechanism for how such dependence may develop. When users repeatedly experience the immediate gratification of high-quality AI outputs, initially voluntary use can gradually transition into more automatic delegation (Limayem et al., 2007; Venkatesh et al., 2012). Oulasvirta et al. (2012) document an analogous pattern in the case of smartphone checking, showing how short reinforcement cycles can harden into habitual behavior. Extending this logic to the GenAI context, users may form delegation habits in which they reflexively turn to the model even for tasks they could manage independently. What begins as a deliberate efficiency choice may therefore settle into an automatic response.A complementary line of argument concerns the psychological consequences of sustained reliance on a system that appears to outperform the user. Over time, repeated exposure to high-quality AI outputs may erode users’ confidence in their own judgment, in a manner broadly consistent with learned-helplessness accounts of reduced self-efficacy under persistent superior-agent conditions (Seligman, 1975). Research on automation more generally has documented a related pattern, in which heavy reliance on decision-support systems is associated reduced independent scrutiny and increased decision errors (J. D. Lee & See, 2004; Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010). For GenAI users, these dynamics may produce a self-reinforcing cycle in which each successful delegation raises the likelihood of the next, quietly consolidating dependence without the user fully noticing. Viewed through this lens, GenAI dependence is best understood as a by-product of sustained collaboration depth. The more central the system becomes to the workflow, the more the division of cognitive labor can tilt toward capability loss in the absence of deliberate safeguards. While conceptually adjacent, habit and dependence warrant analytical separation. Habit reflects the automaticity that emerges through repeated enactment, whereas GenAI dependence denotes a deeper psychological state, one in which users not only default to the system but begin to doubt their capacity to perform competently without it, perceiving the technology as increasingly indispensable to task accomplishment.2.7 Long-Term Orientation in Technology Use and Skill RetentionLTO reflects an orientation that values delayed rewards, planning, and sustained effort toward longer-term goals (Bearden et al., 2006; Hofstede, 2001). In entrepreneurial settings, LTO has been linked to strategic flexibility and patient capability-building, with LTO entrepreneurs showing greater willingness to treat new tools as durable strategic resources rather than as episodic aids (Lumpkin & Brigham, 2011). Applied to GenAI, this temporal orientation is likely to encourage persistent and deep engagement, since high-LTO users are more inclined to see the tool as a long-term investment in competitive capability.This same orientation, however, has opposing implications for skill retention. When GenAI is perceived as essential to long-term competitiveness, users may invest heavily in integrating it into their workflows while paying less attention to the rehearsal cycles that sustain independent expertise. Drawing on temporal self-regulation accounts (Hall & Fong, 2007), we suggest that high-LTO individuals may assign greater weight to the anticipated strategic benefits of sustained GenAI integration, particularly when the potential costs of reduced rehearsal remain uncertain or difficult to observe. As AI-supported workflows become tied to longer-term professional goals, users may assign lower priority to interrupting them through periods of unaided practice. The same future-oriented commitment that supports sustained technology engagement may therefore also strengthen the path from use to dependence. Which trajectory prevails is, we argue, an empirical question shaped by whether users couple their long-term engagement with deliberate practice routines, rather than a property of LTO itself.2.8 Cognitive and Behavioural Mechanisms of Technology DependenceThe perspectives reviewed in the preceding sections each address a distinct aspect of GenAI dependence. Cognitive offloading theory explains the initial tendency to delegate, skill decay theory explains why sustained non-use erodes expertise, and the psychological and temporal frameworks explain who is most likely to travel furthest along this path. Read in isolation, however, each of these mechanisms captures only a fragment of the process. In this section we draw them together into an integrated cognitive-behavioural account of how GenAI use can tilt, over time, toward dependence.At the cognitive level, GenAI prompts voluntary cognitive offloading, as users externalise working-memory operations such as drafting, summarising, and code completion to the model itself (Risko & Gilbert, 2016). This efficiency comes at a cost. When effortful processing is consistently outsourced, users forgo the desirable difficulties through which durable learning is typically consolidated (Bjork & Bjork, 2011). A related risk is that AI-assisted output can be misattributed to one’s own capabilities, which can mask gradual skill decay from the user’s own view.These mis-calibrated cognitions can set in motion a reinforcement loop of a kind familiar from habit-formation research. Early productivity gains tend to reinforce repeated use, and discretionary reliance gradually settles into more automatic delegation (Limayem et al., 2007). Recurrent exposure to what appears to be a superior external agent may, in parallel, erode self-efficacy in ways broadly reminiscent of learned-helplessness dynamics (Seligman, 1975). Viewed over longer time horizons, these patterns are consistent with path-dependence logic (Arthur, s1989): self-reinforcing early choices tend to channel subsequent options and make reversal progressively more costly, as workflows reorganize themselves around the tool and the perceived cost of operating without it rises over time.For entrepreneurially oriented professionals, who adopt GenAI precisely in order to sustain a competitive edge, these dynamics can produce a strategic paradox. The very tools they rely on to enhance short-run agility may, in the longer run, constrain the independent capability on which their adaptability depends. We interpret these linked cognitive, behavioural, and temporal dynamics as candidate micro-foundations of collaboration asymmetry, that is, as the specific processes through which sustained collaboration depth can tilt into dependence.The perspectives reviewed above address different stages of the phenomenon we investigate. Entrepreneurially oriented individuals tend to embrace the tools they regard as levers of competitive advantage (Bharadwaj et al., 2013; Srinivasan et al., 2002), to escalate commitment to chosen courses of action under uncertainty (McCarthy et al., 1993), and to exhibit a pattern-recognition-oriented cognitive style that can tip into overcommitment when opportunity signals are salient (Baron, 2006). These dispositional tendencies, taken together, suggest that IEO may foster psychological attachment to the availability of GenAI through identity and strategic framing, even beyond sheer volume of use. High-LTO individuals tend to reframe routine tool use as long-horizon capability-building, so each usage episode accrues as psychological equity in the tool rather than passing as a one-off convenience. A given behavioural frequency therefore compounds into dependence more quickly under high LTO, because each episode is weighted as a commitment. Under low LTO, usage remains episodic and substitutable; under high LTO, it hardens into path-dependent lock-in.Temporal self-regulation theory (Hall & Fong, 2007) adds a second mechanism by explaining how behaviour is shaped by the perceived timing of costs and benefits. In the GenAI context, the benefits of intensive use are immediately observable, while the potential costs of over-reliance, including reduced autonomy and skill erosion, are gradual, uncertain, and comparatively difficult to detect. When high-LTO individuals interpret GenAI integration as an investment in future competitiveness, they may persist with established AI-supported workflows and assign less immediate priority to maintaining parallel, unaided practice routines. This persistence can weaken the corrective feedback that might otherwise prevent repeated use from gradually developing into dependence.
