In contrast, the indirect path from individual entrepreneurial orientation to perceived skill atrophy through GenAI dependence alone, bypassing usage intensity, was not significant (β = 0.048, 95% CI [− 0.034, 0.157], p = 0.311), indicating that the shorter pathway was not supported.The moderated-mediation index, capturing the indirect effect of the Long-Term Orientation × Gen AI Usage Intensity interaction on skill atrophy via GenAI dependence, was positive and significant (β = 0.084, 95% CI [0.018, 0.160], p = 0.022). This extends H3 by showing that long-term orientation’s amplification of the usage-to-dependence path propagates downstream to skill atrophy: individuals high in long-term orientation experience stronger conversion of usage into dependence and, consequently, greater perceived erosion of professional skills.6 DiscussionOur investigation set out to examine how individual entrepreneurial orientation relates to the depth of human-AI collaboration, captured through GenAI usage intensity, and how this collaboration depth relates to GenAI dependence and perceived skill atrophy.Our findings indicate that, in this sample, individual entrepreneurial orientation was positively associated with collaboration depth and that long-term orientation strengthened the positive association between collaboration depth and dependence. Whether safeguards can attenuate these relationships remains an important question for future research.This study paints a nuanced portrait. On the one hand, individual entrepreneurial orientation is associated with a propensity to act boldly and experiment with emerging technologies, which helps explain why entrepreneurially oriented professionals may engage more deeply with GenAI. On the other hand, those very gains may conceal a slower-burn process in which cognitive off-loading, habituation, and temporal commitment converge in ways that are associated with perceived erosion of human expertise as human-AI collaboration is perceived to drift from augmentation toward substitution. This pattern reflects what we term the “hustle-to-handicap” paradox: the same proactiveness, innovativeness, and willingness to experiment that encourage entrepreneurially oriented professionals to integrate GenAI deeply into their work may, through sustained use, foster dependence and perceived erosion of professional capability.Our evidence is consistent with the theorized sequential pathway: higher individual entrepreneurial orientation is associated with greater collaboration depth (GenAI Usage Intensity), which is associated with collaboration asymmetry (GenAI Dependence); this dependence, in turn, is associated with perceived skill atrophy. The pathway from usage intensity to dependence and, ultimately, skill atrophy is consistent with the central mechanism theorized in our model and accounts for a meaningful share of the observed variance. The individual entrepreneurial orientation to dependence path clarifies an important boundary condition of our model.We proposed two channels linking entrepreneurial orientation to GenAI dependence: a behavioral channel operating through sustained usage (H1a and H1b) and a direct disposition-level channel (H2). The results support the first but not the second. The direct path from individual entrepreneurial orientation to GenAI dependence was not statistically significant (β = 0.099, p = 0.288), whereas the indirect effect of individual entrepreneurial orientation on GenAI dependence through GenAI usage intensity was significant (β = 0.149, 95% CI [0.057, 0.262], p = 0.004). Following Zhao et al.’s (2010) the mediation framework, this pattern is consistent with indirect-only mediation for GenAI sependence rather than a partial-mediation account. The findings therefore suggest that, in this sample, entrepreneurial orientation was associated with GenAI sependence primarily through its relationship with sustained and intensive GenAI use rather than through a direct disposition-level pathway. Theoretically, this refines the explanatory account by indicating that GenAI dependence is linked more closely to the behavioral enactment of entrepreneurial orientation than to disposition alone. This distinction also carries practical implications: professionals high in individual entrepreneurial orientation may be more vulnerable to dependence when their entrepreneurial orientation is expressed through deeper and sustained GenAI engagement, particularly where safeguards for independent practice are limited.At the heart of this paradox lies a double-edged mechanism: the very features that make GenAI appealing also engender over-reliance. Prior research extols individual entrepreneurial orientation as a strategic resource that enhances opportunity spotting, risk taking, and proactiveness (Bolton & Lane, 2012; Wales, 2016). Yet the same cognitive scripts that favor swift experimentation may, under conditions of pervasive AI support, contribute to over-reliance when sustained engagement is not balanced by independent practice. Heavy reliance on GenAI may shift problem-solving from effortful sense-making to automated pattern completion, aligning with the cognitive off-loading framework (Risko & Gilbert, 2016). The observed usage-to-dependence relationship is consistent with repeated cognitive offloading, although offloading itself was not directly measured. Professionals high in long-term orientation may interpret sustained GenAI use as a strategically rational investment, making these routines harder to reverse over time.At first glance, entrepreneurial and future-focused professionals seem unlikely candidates for technology overdependence: they are proactive, experimental, and keen to future-proof their workflows. Our evidence complicates that intuition. Individual entrepreneurial orientation may encourage intensive delegation to GenAI, while long-term orientation may strengthen the conversion of such delegation into dependence. If left unbalanced, this pattern may reconfigure skills in ways that matter for the future of work.This potential lock-in has important ramifications for the canonical debate on human-AI complementarities. GenAI rarely enters workflows as a substitute technology. It typically arrives as an augmentative collaborator, woven into existing practice rather than displacing it. The concern animating this study, then, is not substitution as such, but the conditions under which repeated augmentation may gradually approach functional substitution through the deepening of dependence. Much of the information systems literature frames intelligent systems as potential amplifiers of human judgment, emphasizing complementarity between algorithmic capabilities and human expertise (Dellermann et al., 2019; Raisch & Krakowski, 2021; Seeber et al., 2020). Meta-analytic evidence already tempers this optimism. Across 106 experiments, Vaccaro et al. (2024) find that human-AI combinations performed on average worse than the better of human or AI alone, with losses concentrated in decision-making tasks and gains in content creation, which indicates that complementarity is a contingent outcome rather than a property of the combination itself. Our results complicate that optimism by suggesting a dynamic continuum along which complementarity may, in users’ perceptions, give way to substitution. When GenAI outputs become indispensable cognitive crutches, the human role migrates from active interpretation to passive oversight, heightening vulnerability to automation bias and complacency (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010). Complementarity is therefore not an inherent property of adoption but an emergent state of the digital work configuration that must be actively maintained through collaboration design and practice.An important boundary condition in our argument concerns how GenAI is introduced into the workflow. We did not capture whether respondents used tools they selected themselves or tools provided by their employers, yet this distinction affects how the underlying mechanism should be interpreted. Self-selected use is more voluntary and may become more closely tied to users’ identities, consistent with the concept of information technology identity (Carter & Grover, 2015). It may also create conditions conducive to psychological ownership (Pierce et al., 2001) and, through repeated, comprehensive, voluntary use, to habit formation (Limayem et al., 2007). Together, these conditions may make the strategic-investment logic underlying our long-term orientation moderation more salient. By contrast, mandated use may be frequent but remain externally regulated, meaning that high behavioral engagement does not necessarily translate into the felt compulsion captured by our dependence construct.The mode of provisioning may also shape the downstream effects of dependence. Employer-sanctioned deployments may be accompanied by formal usage protocols, verification requirements, and managerial oversight, whereas self-directed use may occur with fewer structured safeguards. Whether such arrangements preserve independent judgment and opportunities for skill rehearsal likely depends on how these governance mechanisms are designed and implemented. More broadly, research on connected workplace surveillance and digital productivity tools suggests that the depth and nature of human-AI engagement are shaped partly by organizational governance and control rather than by technical features alone (Mettler, 2024; Nyman et al., 2024). Some dependence indicators, particularly concealment and concern expressed by others, may also carry different meanings where GenAI use is organizationally expected rather than discretionary.The characteristics of our sample provide some indication that use was predominantly self-directed. Specifically, 60.1% of respondents reported using only free versions of GenAI tools, while 67.8% reported using two or more tools. The use of free versions and multiple tools suggests self-directed adoption but does not establish the provisioning regime. Because the survey did not directly measure whether GenAI use was self-selected or employer-mandated, the findings should not be restricted to either regime. Provisioning should instead be treated as an unobserved boundary condition for future research.A second boundary condition relates to the organizational setting in which these individual orientations are expressed. Although we model individual entrepreneurial orientation and long-term orientation as personal dispositions, such dispositions are more likely to shape behavior when the surrounding environment supports them. For example, an organizational culture that encourages experimentation and accepts failure may strengthen the relationship between individual entrepreneurial orientation and collaboration depth. In contrast, a culture that discourages deviation may prevent an entrepreneurial disposition from translating into actual behavior.Long-term orientation is also closely tied to context. It was originally developed as a cultural construct (Hofstede, 1980, 2001) and has also been examined at the firm level as a strategic orientation (Lumpkin & Brigham, 2011). Our individual-level measure, therefore, captures only one expression of a construct that also operates at organizational and national levels. It is also possible that individuals are drawn to organizations whose cultures match their own dispositions. In that case, organizational culture may influence both entrepreneurial orientation and access to GenAI, creating a common source of variation that our research design cannot fully rule out. We therefore interpret our findings as individual-level associations observed across diverse organizational settings and view cross-level theorizing as an important direction for future research.Theoretically, the hustle-to-handicap dynamic integrates three streams of scholarship. First, it extends entrepreneurial cognition research by suggesting that pattern-recognition strengths (Baron, 2006) may become associated with diminished independent capability when amplified by sustained GenAI reliance. Second, it bridges automation bias theory with temporal self-regulation theory (Hall & Fong, 2007), suggesting that individuals with a stronger long-term orientation may frame sustained GenAI use as a strategic investment, which may strengthen the progression from usage to dependence. Third, the argument resonates with organizational-learning research showing that knowledge creation and retention depend on the relationship between experience and organizational context (Argote & Miron-Spektor, 2011). In GenAI-enabled work, systematically bypassing unaided practice may alter the experience through which professional knowledge is retained. We add to human-AI collaboration research by identifying collaboration depth and collaboration asymmetry as micro-foundations of capability reconfiguration.Longitudinal multi-method research should track objective skill metrics alongside psychometric measures of dependence. Candidate metrics include coding-challenge scores and clinical-diagnosis accuracy, which would help establish whether productivity peaks precede persistent skill decline. Qualitative process studies could explore the identity work professionals undertake as they confront perceived capability deterioration (Petriglieri, 2012). Cross-level theorizing is needed to test how organizational learning climates, AI explanation transparency, or regulatory regimes modulate the complementarity-substitution shift. Experimental manipulations of interface friction (for example, forced retrieval prompts) could illuminate design levers that preserve human agency without sacrificing efficiency.Building on these prospective avenues, we situate our results within the study’s theoretical scaffolding. Our findings are consistent with cognitive-offloading theory. The positive indirect effect of GenAI usage intensity on skill atrophy through GenAI dependence mirrors the theory’s prediction that frequent outsourcing suppresses the rehearsal processes that sustain expertise (Risko & Gilbert, 2016). Moreover, the moderating effect of long-term orientation reveals a paradoxical twist: future-focused professionals may double down on offloading because they view GenAI as a strategic asset, increasing vulnerability to perceived competence erosion. In short, the findings are consistent with a field-based account of cognitive offloading.Our findings also speak to the positioning of GenAI within the longer arc of the technology-dependence literature. The pattern we document, in which a meaningful usage-to-dependence path is accompanied by a strong dependence-to-atrophy path operating through professional skills, is broadly consistent in structure with dependence patterns that have been reported across prior technology waves. These include deskilling in process control (Bainbridge, 1983; Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010), transactive memory offloading in the context of internet search (Sparrow et al., 2011), and the cognitive displacement effects reported for smartphones (Ward et al., 2017). What appears to distinguish our evidence is not the existence of dependence as such, since dependence is a structural feature of tool-mediated cognition more generally, but the breadth and cognitive depth of the capabilities that seem to be implicated. Prior technologies tended to substitute for domain-specific cognitive functions, whereas our participants report a broader perceived erosion of their professional skills. This pattern is consistent with the theoretical argument that GenAI’s distinctiveness lies in its generativity and breadth rather than in any fundamentally novel mechanism. The underlying dynamic is one that automation research has been tracing for decades. What appears to have shifted is the scope of what is being offloaded. Our findings, therefore, extend the technology-dependence tradition into the domain of generative cognitive work while preserving its core theoretical architecture.More generally, our findings link cognitive offloading with prior work on skill decay and automation-related capability loss. The evidence that dependence is positively associated with perceived skill atrophy (β = 0.488, p < 0.001) is consistent with Arthur et al.’s (1998) claim that sustained disuse leads to skill degradation, and it extends Bainbridge’s (1983) argument from physical automation and process control to the cognitive work that individuals increasingly delegate to GenAI. Cognitive offloading theory is needed to explain why dependence arises in the first place, while skill decay theory explains how that dependence, once established, is associated with perceived skill atrophy. Together, the two theories provide a coherent account of the theorized pathway examined in this study. Integrating the two theories helps specify both the proposed upstream development of dependence and its downstream association with perceived skill atrophy.Our findings sound a cautionary note. The entrepreneurial zeal celebrated in contemporary innovation narratives may, under the accelerating influence of GenAI, introduce latent vulnerabilities into the human capital on which firms depend. Enduring advantage will rest less on whether organizations adopt GenAI than on how they configure, monitor, and periodically rebalance the human-AI collaboration arrangements through which capability is preserved.7 Implications7.1 Implications for ResearchThe study contributes to research by showing that human-AI complementarity should be understood as dynamic rather than static. GenAI may support productivity in the short run, but sustained collaboration can become asymmetric when usage becomes associated with dependence. The findings also identify GenAI dependence as the mechanism linking collaboration depth with perceived skill atrophy, thereby connecting cognitive offloading theory with the skill decay literature. In doing so, the study responds to the observation that research on human-AI augmentation remains fragmented across management disciplines (Nguyen & Elbanna, 2025). Finally, the study extends the broader technology-dependence tradition by showing that GenAI is continuous with earlier concerns around automation, internet search, and smartphones, while being distinctive in the breadth and generativity of the cognitive work it supports.The study also contributes to research on entrepreneurial orientation by showing that IEO is not directly associated with GenAI Dependence but is linked to dependence through sustained GenAI usage. This distinction helps separate disposition from enacted behavior and suggests that entrepreneurial orientation becomes consequential when translated into concrete collaboration practices. In addition, the moderation result positions LTO as a boundary condition that can intensify the usage-to-dependence relationship, thereby extending temporal self-regulation and path-dependence perspectives into the context of GenAI-enabled work.7.2 Implications for PracticeGenAI can boost productivity, yet our findings suggest that deeper human-AI collaboration may be associated with GenAI dependence and, ultimately, perceived skill atrophy when not accompanied by deliberate safeguards. To prevent this drift, organizations should institutionalize AI-free rehearsal windows, that is, regularly scheduled periods when knowledge workers must complete pivotal tasks without GenAI assistance. Learning research suggests that unaided retrieval and practice can create desirable difficulties that support durable learning (Bjork & Bjork, 2011), while cognitive-offloading research highlights how reliance on external aids can reduce internal processing demands (Risko & Gilbert, 2016).GenAI dependence may remain difficult to recognize until organizations assess patterns of task-level reliance. Organizations could use employee self-assessments, workflow reviews, or appropriately aggregated usage data to identify areas in which independent capability may require reinforcement. Any such assessment should be proportionate, transparent, and subject to privacy safeguards, with the primary purpose of capability development rather than employee surveillance. Such assessments presuppose that organizations have visibility into the tools their employees use. Where adoption is self-directed and occurs outside sanctioned provisioning, such instrumentation is difficult to implement, and the first governance task is to establish visibility rather than to schedule rehearsal. Organizations should therefore distinguish between employer-mandated and self-selected GenAI use when designing monitoring, verification, and skill-retention safeguards. Mandated use may require formal capability-preservation routines and verification protocols, whereas self-selected use may require greater attention to unobserved reliance, unsanctioned workflows, and employees’ ability to work independently of the technology.Our moderated-mediation results suggest that employees with a strong LTO may convert a given amount of usage into disproportionately greater dependence. Framing periodic manual practice as a future-proofing investment may make safeguards more acceptable to high-LTO users and help align skill-maintenance incentives with the very temporal outlook that otherwise accelerates lock-in.At the individual entrepreneur level, founders should maintain active collaboration competence through brief, regular AI-off sprints and a simple delegation log, so exploration does not silently erode core craft. Individuals high in IEO may be inclined toward deeper collaboration, and a stronger LTO may intensify commitment to such collaboration unless it is paired with explicit safeguards such as AI-off sprints, delegation logs, and capability-floor checks (Bolton & Lane, 2012; Weick & Sutcliffe, 2015). For entrepreneurial ventures, we translate human-AI collaboration into governance of digital work configurations, specifically who (human vs. GenAI) does what, with what oversight and redundancy, under conditions of extreme uncertainty and resource constraint (Dellermann et al., 2019; Edmondson, 2012; Seeber et al., 2020).Founders can draw on effectuation and bricolage to experiment with and recombine the limited resources available to them while maintaining capability floors of GenAI-independent proficiency in the tasks that anchor the venture’s value proposition (Baker & Nelson, 2005; Sarasvathy, 2001). GenAI’s demonstrated speed gains may facilitate faster experimentation; viewed through a lean-startup lens, this could support more rapid MVP cycles and iteration (Dell’Acqua et al., 2023; Ries, 2011). Yet without deliberate rotation, dual-path reviews that combine AI and human judgment, and regular critical-skill drills, that collaboration depth risks hardening into collaboration asymmetry and perceived skill loss. Viewed through the lenses of dynamic capabilities and resource orchestration (Sirmon et al., 2011; Teece et al., 1997), these routines allow start-ups to sense, seize, and reconfigure the human-AI task partition as evidence accumulates. The effect is to scale the benefits of collaboration while preserving the founder’s and team’s expertise.At the ecosystem and investor interface, entrepreneurship policy and capital should enable reversible collaboration choices: portability of prompts/artifacts and open formats reduce vendor lock-in, preserving founders’ option value to reconfigure work as the venture learns (Shapiro & Varian, 1999). Digital entrepreneurial ecosystems that foreground digital affordances can pair such interoperability with emerging safety norms (capability-floor audits, AI-in-the-loop traceability), so accelerators, corporates, and boards can encourage deeper collaboration while reducing the risk of long-run human-capital decay in the talent pool (Autio et al., 2018).8 LimitationsOur study has several limitations. First, a limitation concerns the temporal fit between our model and our method. The hypothesized mechanism is inherently processual. Each stage unfolds as a downstream consequence of the one before it, and SA in particular is not expected to emerge immediately but to accumulate gradually as practice cycles are bypassed. Our two-wave design partially addresses this concern by measuring IEO, GenAI usage intensity, LTO, and the control variables at T1, and GenAI dependence and perceived SA at T2, roughly one week later. This separation reduces common-method concerns and provides a stronger basis for testing the proposed sequence than a single-wave design, but the one-week interval cannot capture the longer developmental trajectory through which GenAI dependence and SA may evolve. Because GenAI dependence and perceived SA were both measured at T2, their temporal ordering cannot be conclusively established.Second, because the country distribution was uneven, we did not estimate country-level or culture-level effects. Instead, we treat the multi-country sample as providing contextual heterogeneity rather than cross-cultural evidence. Accordingly, the findings should be interpreted as individual-level relationships observed across a diverse sample, not as evidence of cross-country or cultural differences.Third, several measurement choices warrant scrutiny. Both GenAI dependence and perceived SA were measured using self-report scales, which are susceptible to social desirability and recall biases (Podsakoff et al., 2003). The present investigation should therefore be construed as an inquiry into perceived skill atrophy, as distinct from any empirical assessment of objective performance degradation. Our perceived-SA scale also sits at the boundary of two related workforce constructs: skill atrophy, which refers to the deterioration of capability through disuse (Arthur Jr et al., 1998), and skill obsolescence, which refers to the perception that one’s skills are no longer adequate to current task or labor-market demands (Pazy, 1996). In the GenAI context, these perceptions are difficult to disentangle. Relatedly, our collaboration-depth index combines hours-based behavioral engagement with identity-centrality items, following Ellison et al. (2007), which leaves its task-structural facets unresolved within the present design.Fourth, skill was operationalized as a single latent construct, a coarse-grained approach that blurs potentially meaningful differences among analytical, creative, and interpersonal competencies.Fifth, the GenAI ecosystem itself is a moving target: model capabilities, cost structures, and organizational guardrails are evolving rapidly. The implications of this volatility for the persistence and generalisability of our findings cannot be adjudicated within the present design.9 Future ResearchFirst, multi-wave panel studies could follow the same individuals over extended periods, ideally analyzed with cross-lagged or latent-growth models and augmented by objective skill benchmarks such as clinical-diagnosis performance (Ployhart & Vandenberg, 2010). Such designs would help test whether the sequential process unfolds as theorized and would also address the reciprocal possibility that GenAI access itself cultivates entrepreneurial orientation (Duong, 2024), a direction that our current design cannot disentangle from the forward channel we test.Second, larger and more balanced samples, with broader representation from under-sampled regions, could examine whether national culture, entrepreneurial ecosystem support, or institutional conditions shape the relationships proposed in our model.Third, future studies could triangulate self-reported perceptions with unobtrusive system-log data, supervisor and peer ratings, and objective performance benchmarks, such as coding-test accuracy and writing-quality audits. Such triangulation would yield a richer multi-source picture. The perceived SA measure, adapted from Ryan and Harrison’s (2001) two-item scale, would particularly benefit from such triangulation, and future replications should also consider longer multi-item alternatives. Future research using purpose-built scales that separately measure capability decline and perceived relevance would also help clarify which of the two constructs operates in the relationships we document. Subsequent work could further decompose the collaboration-depth construct into its task-structural facets, such as the range of tasks delegated, the volume of tokens exchanged, and the degree of iterative co-production between the user and the model, to test whether these facets exert distinct effects on dependence and SA.Fourth, laboratory micro-tasks and field quasi-experiments could test whether specific capabilities decay at distinct rates and whether centaur configurations, workflows in which humans deliberately alternate with AI rather than delegate wholesale, selectively buffer decline in some domains (Brynjolfsson & Mitchell, 2017).Fifth, longitudinal fieldwork spanning successive tool generations could examine whether deliberate de-automation practices, such as scheduled AI-free intervals or friction-inducing interface elements, merely stabilize human expertise or can actively regenerate skills that have already begun to atrophy. Such designs would also illuminate how shifts in corporate policy or regulatory regimes interact with individual behavioral trajectories to amplify or dampen the erosion process.Sixth, future work could treat the provisioning regime as an explicit moderator, comparing self-selected with employer-mandated GenAI deployment. Such designs would clarify whether organizational control of the tool amplifies dependence through enforced workflow lock-in, or attenuates it by substituting compliance for internalized reliance, and whether the governance that typically accompanies sanctioned deployment buffers the dependence-to-atrophy path.Lastly, multilevel designs sampling individuals nested within organizations could test whether entrepreneurial culture, psychological safety, and error tolerance moderate the translation of individual entrepreneurial orientation into collaboration depth, and whether organizational verification norms buffer the dependence-to-atrophy path. Such designs would also permit organizational and individual long-term orientation to be modeled simultaneously, which the present two-wave individual-level design cannot do.10 ConclusionHuman-AI collaboration can drift from complementarity to collaboration asymmetry. Our results are consistent with a theorized sequential pathway: individuals higher in entrepreneurial orientation report deeper collaboration with GenAI; such collaboration is associated with GenAI dependence; and dependence, in turn, is associated with perceived skill erosion. A strong long-term orientation appears to strengthen the usage-to-dependence link, forming the pattern we term the “hustle-to-handicap” paradox. Theoretically, we qualify claims of stable complementarity by identifying dependence as a channel through which collaboration depth may become associated with perceived capability erosion. Managerially, the central implication is skill stewardship: organizations should govern GenAI collaboration to preserve role boundaries, independent verification, and core human capabilities. Governing collaboration depth rather than merely expanding access allows organizations to capture GenAI’s productivity gains while maintaining expertise that is transferable, auditable, and resilient across tool generations. The long-term challenge confronting organizations, then, may not be whether humans collaborate with GenAI, but how such collaboration is governed so that the gains of augmentation are not gradually offset by deepening dependence.
